questions.question:
**The question below consists of a set of labelled sentences. Out of the four options given, select the most logical order of the sentences to form a coherent paragraph.**

It was winter, and on

A-cup of coffee was what

B-that cold day a hot

C-I needed desperately
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **BAC.**

** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__**

The part which comes first in the sequence should suitably follow the preposition *on.* Part B seems to be appropriate. ‘It was winter, and on that cold day…’ seems logically correct.

The next in sequence is the one that follows the adjective *hot*. So, part A seems correct to be second in the sequence followed by part C.

*It was winter, and on that cold day a hot cup of coffee was what I needed desperately*

Thus, the sequence is BAC, making **option 4** the correct answer.

questions.question:
**In the following question, out of the four alternatives, select the alternative which will improve the bracketed part of the sentence. In case no improvement is needed, select "no improvement".**

I cook almost every day, but even the thought of producing that quantum of food (daunt) for me.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is "**is daunting".**

*****__Key Points__****

__
 
• The sentence uses the present tense.
 
• Also, looking at the structure of the sentence in which the first part uses simple present tense (cook), the next part of the sentence can suitably use the verb in present continuous. 
 
• So, **is daunting** should be used. 
 
• The **correct sentence** is- I cook almost every day, but even the thought of producing that quantum of food **is daunting** for me.*

***Additional Information__**

__
 
• The structure of the present tense__ is: Subject+ first form of verb(s,es)
 
• The subject before the word __daunting__ is ‘the thought of producing’ which is singular. So, is daunting *is correct and not *are daunting*.
 
• __Daunting__ means difficult to deal with.
 
• **Here, the word 'daunting' is an adjective. It qualifies the noun 'thought'.**

questions.question:
**In the following question, out of the four alternatives, select the alternative which will improve the bracketed part of the sentence. In case no improvement is needed, select "no improvement".**

He had had a short illness, there (had been) a brief time of acute suffering, then all was over.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is : (4) **No Improvement**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Let us consider a sentence: I have had a meeting with the president.
 
• This sentence is in the present perfect tense__ as it talks about a past action that is continuing into the present.
 
• Here, In this sentence, there are two verbs have and had. 
 
• The first** have** is auxiliary also known as the* helping verb* and the second **had** is the* main action verb.*
 
• A sentence may or may not have an auxiliary verb but it’ll "always" have a main or verb.
 
• Now, when we use the same sentence in past tense it changes to: __ I had had a meeting with the president__. 
 
• The main verb here is ***had*** that’s why we are ending up with "double *had'*.
 
• Some more examples will help us to understand this by changing the tenses from present to past:
 
 
• I have had a busy week - I had had a busy week
 
• She have had some troubles - She had had some troubles
 
 
 
• Now, the first part of the sentence is in the past perfect (had + verb).
 
• Here, the verb is also *had*. (That’s why double had).
 
• The rest of the sentence should also be in the past perfect tense (been is the verb).

Thus, no improvement is required. **Option 4** is the correct answer.

questions.question:
**In the following question, out of the four alternatives, select the alternative which is the best substitute of the words/sentence.**

questions.solution:
The correct answer is "**Jinx".** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**Let us look at the meaning of the given words:

__
 
• **Felicitous **– used to describe something as suitable / right because it expresses the desired thought

 
 
• Example: His felicitous remark during the interview helped him secure the job.
 
 
 
• **Adventitious **– happening by chance or by accident
 
 
• Example: The adventitious discovery of the antique coin in the attic was a pleasant surprise for the homeowner.
 
 
 
• **Jinx** – someone or something that brings bad luck
 
 
• Example: After losing three games in a row, the superstitious player started to believe he was a jinx for the team.
 
 
 
• **Providential **– happening exactly when needed
 
 
• Example: The providential arrival of the search party saved the lost hikers from a freezing night in the mountains.​
 
 

Thus, the word *jinx* expresses the desired meaning, making **option 3** the correct answer.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• It can be used as a *noun* or a *verb.*

 
 
• **Example**: I didn’t want to say anything to him – I was afraid I might jinx__ him. (verb)
 
 
 
• There must be a__ jinx__ on our team – four of our best players were injured yesterday. (noun)
 
• **Synonyms**: voodoo, spell, damn, bewitch, evil-eye, curse, hex

questions.question:
**In the following question, out of the four alternatives, select the alternative which best expresses the meaning of the idiom/phrase.**

Pedal to the metal

options.text: Add more protection to an already strong shield.
Push a person to perform to its extreme.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is: **To drive very fast.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The idiom "pedal to the metal" is often used to describe driving a vehicle at full throttle or with maximum speed.
 
• It implies pushing the accelerator pedal all the way to the floor ("metal" referring to the floorboard of a car).

Thus, the correct answer is **option 3**.

Example: We are going to have to put the** pedal to the metal **if we want to finish on time.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Build something big by yourself:**

 
 
• This option does not express the meaning of the idiom "pedal to the metal." The idiom is related to driving or speed and does not refer to building or creating something.
 
 
 
• **Add more protection to an already strong shield:**
 
 
• This option does not express the meaning of the idiom "pedal to the metal." The idiom is about driving fast and does not involve adding protection to a shield or any form of defensive action.
 
 
 
• **Push a person to perform to its extreme:**
 
 
• This option is somewhat related to the idiom "pedal to the metal." It captures the essence of pushing someone to perform at their maximum or pushing them to their limits. However, it does not specifically convey the notion of speed or driving, which is the primary meaning of the idiom.

questions.question:
**In the following question, out of the four alternatives, select the alternative which best expresses the meaning of the idiom/phrase.**

Tongue in cheek

options.text: In an ironic or insincere way.
Stop yourself from saying something hurtful.
Be gutsy and speak the unpleasant truth.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is **In an ironic or insincere way**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• '**Tongue in cheek**' is an idiom that refers to something that is *not serious, not sincere, and is intended to highlight irony in a funny way*.
 
• This idiom can be used:
 
 
• As an Adjective__:
 __
 
• Example: Her latest film is a firmly **tongue-in-cheek** look at the world of advertising. 
 
• Here, 'tongue-in-cheek' is used as the way of how she looked; hence, it is an adjective__ here.
 
 
 
• As an Adverb: 
 __
 
• Example: Ramesh claimed then he was speaking **tongue-in-cheek.**
 
• Here, 'tongue-in-cheek' is a type of comment; hence, it is a noun__ here.
 
 
 
 
 
• Hence, the correct answer is **option 1**.

​ [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

 
• This phrase is a literal reference to the facial expression created when putting the tongue in one's cheek. It also includes a wink to signify that what is being said is not to be taken seriously. The phrase first appeared in print in "The Fair maid of Perth" by Sir Walter Scott in 1928.

questions.question:
**A sentence has been given in Direct/Indirect Speech. Out of the four given alternatives, select the one which best expresses the same sentence in Indirect/Direct Speech.**

She said to me, “I like your smartphone .”

options.text: She told me that she liked my smartphone.
She said that she like my smartphone.
My smartphone was liked by her.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is **She told me that she liked my smartphone**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• In Direct speech__, the message is conveyed in the words of the author or concerned person.
 
• In __Indirect speech__, the message is conveyed in our words. 
 
• When we convert Direct speech to Indirect speech, we omit the inverted commas.
 
• The conjunction that is added before introducing the words spoken between quotation marks (“…”).
 
• We also use conjunction that before reporting the statement within “ - ” marks in our own words.
 
• The tense of the reported speech in the indirect speech depends upon the tense of the reporting verb in the direct speech. If the reporting verb is in the past tense, the verb in the reported speech undergoes a backshift in tense. Here, 'like' will change into 'liked'.

Thus, applying these fundamental rules, the sentence in the Indirect speech is: *She told me that she liked my smartphone.*

*​**​ [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__***

__
 
• Some notable changes that are made while doing the conversion from Direct to Indirect are:​
 
• 
 
 
 

 **Simple Present**
 **Simple Past**
 
 

 Eats
 Ate
 
 

 **Present Continuous**
 **Past Continous**
 
 

 Is eating
 Was eating
 
 

 Present Perfect Continuous
 Past Perfect
 
 

 Is eating
 Was eating
 
 

 **Simple Past**
 ​Past Perfect
 
 

 Has eaten
 Had eaten
 
 
 
 

 

 

 

 

 

 
• **am** changes to **was**, **now **changes to **then**, **tomorrow** changes to** the next day,** etc.
 
• **said to me*** *in Direct speech,__ it changes to **told me** in the __Indirect speech__.

• ​When the subject is being acted upon by the verb – it is __Passive__ Voice.

 Active voice
 Passive voice 
 
 

 Subject + verb + object
 Object + verb + Subject

 Active Voice

With her ______ the gate, you cannot ignore the issue any further.
questions.solution:

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The right preposition to be used here is at.
 
• **At** is a preposition that is used in many cases according to context.
 
• Here, **at** is used in the context of being nearby of something__.
 __
 
• Example__: The teacher is standing at the blackboard.
 __
 
• Here, the sentence implies that the teacher is near__ the board, not __on__ the blackboard.
 
 
 
 
 
• **Hence, the complete sentence is:** *With her **at** the gate, you cannot ignore the issue any further.*

*​ [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__***

__
 
• Other cases where **at** can be used are:

 
 
• Before names of towns/villages -
 
 
• Example__: Seema lives **at** Baroda, a small town in Alwar.
 
 
 
• To indicate the place in which something or somebody is/was/will be -
 __
 
• Example__: In the evening, Hari was **at** his uncle's house.
 
 
 
• To indicate a point of time - 
 __
 
• Example__: I can repay the amount at any moment.

questions.question:
**In the following question, some part of the sentence may have errors. Find out which part of the sentence has an error and select the appropriate option. If a sentence is free from error, select ‘No Error’.**

We can make donations to NGOs (1)/that are engaged in planting trees, (2)/or in anyway work towards saving the environment. (3)/No error (4)
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **3- the error lies in only Part 3.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The error lies in part 3 of the sentence, making **option 3** the correct answer.
 
• The word **anyway** means: in spite of something that has been mentioned before.
 
 
• Example: It was raining heavily, but we drove to the mall** anyway**.
 
 
 
• * ***Any** means one or some of a thing.
 
 
• Example: Do you have **any** food left?
 
 
 
• The speaker here refers to any work towards saving the environment.
 
• There is no point to highlight in spite o__f in the given sentence. So, the use of **any way** is incorrect.
 
• **Hence, the correct sentence is:** *We can make donations to NGOs that are engaged in planting trees or in **any work** towards saving the environment.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 Than
